title: Transgender Military Ban: Thousands of Troops Discharged for Gender Identity
description_medium: President Trump’s January 27, 2025, executive order directed the Pentagon to revise policy affecting transgender service members. The Supreme Court allowed the administration to enforce the ban while litigation continued, and the Defense Department then issued implementation guidance. Those steps do not establish that thousands had already been discharged; the title’s completed-discharge claim needs a dated count and evidence of separations.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed the executive order Prioritizing Military Excellence and Readiness on January 27, 2025. It directed the Defense Department to change eligibility standards for people with gender dysphoria and revoked the prior administration’s policy permitting transgender people to serve openly. The order described its rationale in terms of military readiness and standards; transgender service members and advocacy groups challenged the policy in court. On May 6, 2025, the Supreme Court allowed the government to enforce the ban while the legal cases proceeded. The Pentagon subsequently issued implementation guidance, including a deadline for active-duty personnel to identify themselves and seek voluntary separation. These are distinct stages: signing an order, obtaining interim authority to enforce it, issuing Pentagon guidance, and actually completing separations. The supplied AP account describes troops being identified for removal and reports the government’s estimates of personnel who identified as transgender or had a gender-dysphoria diagnosis. It does not establish that thousands had already been discharged. The entry can document the policy and implementation process, but the existing title states a completed outcome that requires a supported separation total.
evidence_notes: AP reports identification/removal policy and implementation timeline; DoD briefing describes guidance. The order and interim Supreme Court action do not establish completed discharge totals.
corrected_wording: Consider title: “Trump Order Directs Exclusion of Transgender Service Members; Pentagon Begins Implementation.”

title: SAVE Program Weaponized to Flag 67 Million Voter Registrations as Suspect
description_medium: The Trump administration expanded DHS’s SAVE immigration-status system for election officials to compare voter registrations with federal records. By June 2026, at least 67 million registrations had been scanned, and a federal judge blocked the revised tool, citing privacy and wrongful-purge risks; AP reported that Texas voter Anthony Nel had been wrongly flagged. On September 25, 2026, the Supreme Court temporarily lifted that restriction while litigation continued, so the June block is not the current procedural status.
description_long: The Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements system was created to verify immigration status for benefits and later adapted for election-related citizenship checks. AP reported that at least 67 million voter registrations had been scanned through the expanded system and described Anthony Nel, a naturalized U.S. citizen in Texas whose registration was temporarily canceled after a SAVE match incorrectly flagged him. In June 2026, a federal judge barred use of the revamped database, finding risks to privacy and eligible voters. That ruling did not remain the latest procedural action: on September 25, the Supreme Court put the restriction on hold, allowing the administration’s system to be used while the case proceeds. The Supreme Court’s interim order is not a final determination that the system is accurate or lawful. The record supports describing the scale of the scans, the documented false match, the district court’s concerns and the later temporary stay. The title’s word “weaponized” characterizes intent beyond those specific facts, while the figure of 67 million refers to registrations scanned, not registrations found to be ineligible.
evidence_notes: AP documents at least 67 million scans, Nel’s wrongful flag, June injunction; AP/Reuters report Supreme Court stay on Sept 25, 2026. Scans are not flagged noncitizens; no basis to claim all or most were suspect.
corrected_wording: Consider neutral title: “Expanded SAVE System Scans 67 Million Voter Registrations; Courts Review Its Use.”

title: 'Tim Apple' Gaffe: Trump Misnames Tim Cook in White House Meeting
description_medium: During a March 6, 2019, White House meeting on American jobs and the economy, President Donald Trump praised Apple chief executive Tim Cook and then called him “Tim Apple.” Cook was seated beside Trump at the meeting. The remark was an apparent verbal slip, not an announced policy or formal renaming, and the clip quickly circulated in news coverage and online discussion.
description_long: President Donald Trump made the “Tim Apple” remark during a White House meeting on the American Workforce Policy Advisory Board on March 6, 2019. Apple chief executive Tim Cook attended the session, where Trump praised Apple’s investments and its role in expanding U.S. manufacturing. While addressing Cook, Trump used the name “Tim Apple,” apparently combining the executive’s first name with the company’s name. The brief exchange was recorded and quickly became widely discussed as a verbal gaffe. The phrase circulated in news reports, social media posts and jokes, while Cook later changed his display name on Twitter to “Tim Apple.” The incident attracted attention because it occurred in a formal White House setting during a public discussion of jobs, technology and business investment. It did not announce a change to Apple’s leadership, establish a policy decision, or show that Cook had changed his name. The evidence supports describing the remark and the setting, while broader claims that the episode demonstrates a pattern or had material consequences would require additional evidence.
evidence_notes: CNBC directly documents remark and meeting context; maintain this as a discrete public gaffe. No policy effect supported.

title: Trump's 77% trade-deficit reduction claim relies on selective monthly comparison
description_medium: In January 2026, Trump said the U.S. trade deficit had fallen by 77%. FactCheck.org traced that figure to a comparison of monthly deficits in January and October 2025, rather than a full-year comparison. After annual data became available, the site reported that the 2025 goods-and-services deficit was 0.2% below 2024. The two comparisons use different periods and should not be presented as equivalent measures of an annual reduction.
description_long: President Donald Trump said in January 2026 that his policies had reduced the U.S. trade deficit by 77 percent. FactCheck.org examined the figure and found it came from comparing the monthly deficit in January 2025 with the deficit in October 2025. A comparison between two selected months can show a change over that interval, but it does not by itself describe the change across an entire year. In a later analysis using full-year data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, FactCheck.org reported that the combined goods-and-services trade deficit for 2025 was 0.2 percent lower than in 2024. These figures answer different questions: the 77-percent claim uses a pair of monthly observations, while the annual comparison measures the total for each calendar year. The entry is about how the administration presented the trade data and how the fact-check evaluated that presentation. It does not establish that every month moved in the same direction or identify a single cause for the year-to-year change. The stored event date should also be reviewed because the cited claim and fact-check were published in 2026.
evidence_notes: FactCheck.org explains the January-to-October monthly comparison and reports 0.2% full-year decline vs 2024 from BEA data. Existing date field predates claim; separate metadata correction.
corrected_wording: Date should reflect the January 2026 claim or February 2026 fact-check, not November 2025.

title: WLF Accepts $100M From British Money Laundering Suspect, Routes $75M to Trumps
description_medium: Reuters reported in July 2025 that UAE-linked Aqua 1 had agreed to buy $100 million of World Liberty Financial tokens, becoming the venture’s largest publicly disclosed investor. Reuters also described the venture’s revenue arrangement, under which a Trump-affiliated entity was entitled to 75% of net proceeds after expenses. That contractual allocation does not show that $75 million from Aqua 1’s purchase was paid directly to the Trump family.
description_long: Reuters reported that Aqua 1, which described itself as a UAE-based investment venture, announced in late June 2025 that it had purchased $100 million of World Liberty Financial tokens. The purchase made Aqua 1 the largest publicly known investor in the Trump family-linked crypto venture at that time. Reuters separately described World Liberty’s token-sale economics: an entity affiliated with the Trump family was entitled to receive 75 percent of net proceeds after expenses under the company’s revenue arrangement. That general allocation is not evidence that $75 million from Aqua 1’s transaction had already been transferred to the family or its company. Reuters also reported that the Abu Dhabi Global Market said Aqua 1 was not registered, licensed or affiliated with it, despite Aqua 1’s public claims about a regional presence. The supplied article does not support calling the investor a British money-laundering suspect, or the later assertion that a July 2026 investigation identified its principal as Bobby Zhou and traced the money. Those claims need separate, correctly matched reporting or transaction records. The available account supports the disclosed purchase and the potential conflict created by the revenue structure, while the direct routing and investor criminal-history claims remain unestablished here.
evidence_notes: Reuters 2025 source supports $100m token purchase, Aqua 1’s status statement from Abu Dhabi Global Market, and 75% net-proceeds entitlement. Does not establish direct $75m payout, British suspect status, 2026 investigation, or Bobby Zhou claim.
corrected_wording: The title should be narrowed to the disclosed investment and revenue share unless recipient-specific payment records and independently sourced legal-status reporting are added.
exact_blocker: The linked Reuters report does not establish that Aqua 1’s principal was a British money-laundering suspect or that $75 million from this purchase was routed to the Trump family; suitable same-transaction evidence is absent from the packet.

title: DOJ Indicts NY AG Letitia James on Trumped-Up Fraud Charges
description_medium: A federal grand jury indicted New York Attorney General Letitia James in October 2025 on mortgage-related bank-fraud and false-statement charges. James pleaded not guilty. On November 24, a federal judge dismissed the indictment after finding that prosecutor Lindsey Halligan had been unlawfully appointed and lacked authority to bring the case. Reuters later reported that a grand jury rejected an effort to re-indict James. The dismissal concerned the prosecutor’s appointment, not a trial finding on the mortgage allegations.
description_long: The Justice Department brought a federal mortgage-related criminal case against New York Attorney General Letitia James in October 2025. The indictment charged bank fraud and making false statements in connection with a mortgage; James pleaded not guilty and denied wrongdoing. On November 24, U.S. District Judge Cameron McGowan Currie dismissed the case after concluding that Lindsey Halligan, the prosecutor who secured the indictment, had been unlawfully appointed as interim U.S. attorney and did not have legal authority to bring it. The judge set aside the indictment on that procedural basis rather than deciding the truth of the mortgage allegations at trial. Reuters subsequently reported that a grand jury rejected a second attempt to indict James in December. These developments are relevant to the prosecution’s status, but they do not establish that the original allegations were true or false. The existing phrase “Trumped-Up” states a conclusion about motive and merits that is not proved by the indictment or the dismissal alone. The supplied AP link concerns a separate Georgia election investigation and cannot support this event; the description therefore relies on contemporaneous reporting about the James case and its dismissal.
evidence_notes: Reuters sources document indictment, Nov 24 dismissal for unlawful appointment, and Dec 4 grand-jury rejection. The linked AP Georgia case is unrelated. Do not state as established that prosecution was retaliatory or allegations false.
corrected_wording: Consider neutral title: “Letitia James Indicted in Mortgage Case; Judge Dismisses Charges Over Prosecutor’s Appointment.”

title: EO Bans Transgender People from Military Service
description_medium: On January 27, 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing the Pentagon to revise its service policy for transgender people, including people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. It revoked an earlier order permitting open service and set out the administration’s readiness rationale. The Supreme Court allowed enforcement while litigation continued in May 2025, after which the Pentagon issued implementation guidance. The order and court action describe policy steps, not a verified total of completed discharges.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed the executive order Prioritizing Military Excellence and Readiness on January 27, 2025. The order directed the Defense Department to change military eligibility standards affecting transgender people, particularly those with a current or past diagnosis of gender dysphoria, and revoked the earlier policy that had permitted open service. It presented the administration’s rationale in terms of readiness, discipline and standards. Service members and civil-rights groups challenged the policy in federal court. On May 6, 2025, the Supreme Court allowed the administration to enforce the ban while those challenges continued; a later Defense Department memo outlined how the services should implement the policy and set a June deadline for active-duty personnel to identify themselves for voluntary separation. Those events show that the policy moved from executive direction to interim judicial authorization and Pentagon implementation. They do not by themselves show that every affected service member was discharged or establish the eventual number separated. Claims about a specific affected-person count, post-order outcomes or individual military records should be tied to the relevant Pentagon data and date. The White House fact sheet documents the administration’s explanation, while the AP and DoD accounts provide reporting on implementation and litigation.
evidence_notes: White House source supports order language; AP/DoD support May implementation framework. Keep policy order separate from completed separations.
corrected_wording: If title asserts a completed ban or discharges, specify whether it describes the order, implementation policy, or actual separations as of a dated source.

title: Trump Retaliates Against Brad Raffensperger and Election Officials Who Refused to Overturn 2020
description_medium: In March 2025, Trump said people he blamed for the 2020 election “should go to jail.” The Brennan Center also documented an executive order directing a review of former CISA director Christopher Krebs, who had rejected claims that the election was stolen. These sources establish the rhetoric and review directive, but do not establish the separate Georgia party, endorsement and 2026 threat episodes included in the previous account or prove a coordinated campaign against Brad Raffensperger.
description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Donald Trump said that people he blamed for the 2020 election “should go to jail.” The Brennan Center for Justice reported the remark as part of a broader pattern of threats directed at election officials who had administered the 2020 vote. The organization also documented Trump’s executive order directing the Justice Department to review actions by former Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency director Christopher Krebs. Krebs had publicly rejected claims that the 2020 election was rigged or stolen while serving in the first Trump administration. The order named Krebs and called for scrutiny of his conduct, making the review an official action after his public defense of the election’s security. The cited material supports recording Trump’s statement and the Krebs review directive. It does not, by itself, establish the separate claims about a Georgia Republican Party resolution, a gubernatorial endorsement, a 2026 bomb threat, or a specific retaliatory act against Brad Raffensperger. Nor does it establish the private motive behind every government action. Those episodes should be linked to their own dated records if retained. The description therefore distinguishes documented statements and directives from unverified assertions of a coordinated retaliation apparatus.
evidence_notes: Brennan Center supports March 14 remark and Krebs review; does not substantiate other Georgia/2026 claims in populated text. Avoid attribution of motive as settled fact.
corrected_wording: Consider title narrowed to the documented statement and Krebs review; add direct sources for Raffensperger-specific actions.

title: WOTUS Gutted — Trump Rule Would Strip Federal Protection From 80% of U.S. Wetlands
description_medium: On November 17, 2025, EPA and the Army Corps announced a proposed Clean Water Act rule narrowing the definition of “waters of the United States.” The proposal would alter which streams, wetlands and other waters qualify for federal jurisdiction, including a surface-water condition for certain adjacent wetlands. EPA said its analysis could not reliably quantify the nationwide reduction in jurisdiction; the cited 81% estimate is an outside inference from acreage figures, not the agency’s formal estimate.
description_long: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works Adam Telle announced a proposed revision to the definition of “waters of the United States” on November 17, 2025. The definition determines which waters fall under federal Clean Water Act programs, including permitting and pollution controls. The agencies said the proposal was intended to clarify the statute after the Supreme Court’s 2023 Sackett decision and to narrow federal jurisdiction. Under the proposal, certain wetlands would qualify as adjacent waters only if they abut a jurisdictional water and have surface water at least during the wet season. The proposal was published in the Federal Register on November 20 and opened for public comment. EPA’s impact analysis discussed mapped wetland acres and whether they met the proposed criteria, but the agency stated that it could not reliably quantify the proposal’s nationwide reduction in jurisdiction. A legal analysis derived an estimate near 81 percent from the acreage figures; that is not an official EPA finding that 81 percent of all U.S. wetlands would lose protection. The entry should describe the proposed change as a proposal and distinguish the agency’s own assessment from outside calculations. The rulemaking continued through later supplemental notice activity, so this 2025 proposal should not be presented as a final rule.
evidence_notes: EPA source supports Nov17 proposal, 45-day comment period and surface-water condition; EPA said nationwide reduction cannot reliably be quantified. 81% is outside-derived inference from legal analysis, not agency estimate. EPA posted a supplemental proposed rule in 2026; 2025 proposal was not final.
corrected_wording: Clarify in title that the 80% figure is an external estimate and the rule was proposed, not finalized.

title: RFK Jr.'s HHS Unleashes Anti-Vaccine Conspiracy Orthodoxy, Triggers Worst Measles Crisis in 33 Years
description_medium: On June 9, 2025, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 sitting members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and said the panel would be reconstituted. ACIP advises the CDC on vaccine recommendations, and Reuters reported that Kennedy planned to name replacements. This membership change drew concern from public-health experts about the committee’s independence; the linked reporting does not show that it caused the 2025 measles outbreak or prove the title’s causal claim.
description_long: On June 9, 2025, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced that all 17 members of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices would be removed and replaced. ACIP is an expert advisory body that reviews evidence and makes recommendations that inform CDC vaccine guidance. Kennedy said the reset was intended to restore public trust and address what he described as conflicts of interest; public-health experts and vaccine-law specialists questioned the decision, noting that the committee had established conflict-of-interest safeguards and that its work was not partisan. Reuters reported that Kennedy had already announced a change to COVID-19 vaccine recommendations without the committee’s usual consultation, and that the panel was scheduled to meet later in June. He subsequently appointed new members, some of whom had publicly criticized vaccines. The removal altered the membership and governance of a key federal advisory body, which could affect how recommendations are reviewed and communicated. However, the cited Reuters report does not establish that the dismissal caused the later measles outbreak, reduced vaccination rates, or produced the other outcomes named in the existing title and longer draft. Those claims require separate sources and causal evidence. The available record supports the committee’s dismissal and the debate over its independence, not the asserted crisis outcome.
evidence_notes: Reuters/HHS support June 9 removal and stated rationale; Reuters subsequent report covers replacement choices. Does not support causal claim linking removal to measles surge or all claims in title.
corrected_wording: Narrow title to ACIP membership removal and the resulting dispute over advisory independence unless distinct evidence supports measles-related claims.
